content.thinking:
I need to write the whole module carefully in one pass without executing anything. Since the builder likely requires at least one joint to resolve bones against, I'll make sure to create a root joint at the origin so nothing breaks if no joints are defined.

For the layout, I'm planning a stone floor slab as the base with props sitting on top, and designing a chest prop with a body, a hinged lid using a rotated cylinder to fake a curved lathe shape, and iron bands as slightly larger boxes layered over the body.

I'm adding dungeon atmosphere now: a gold lock plate and keyhole, scattered coins and a key near the closed chest, and a back stone wall segment with two wall-mounted torches plus a standing torch, all built from stacked tapering glowing boxes to simulate flame.

For the floor props, I'm placing three barrels using lathe-profile geometry with bulging wood bodies and thin iron hoop rings, including one lying on its side rotated to add visual variety among the standing barrels.

Still defining hoop geometry...

Still writing stave shading logic...

Now I'm planning the bone pile: a skull built from boxes (cranium, jaw, eye sockets) with a small pixel-texture face plane for eyes/nose/teeth, plus scattered femurs made as rods with knob spheres at each end using a bone color.

For the ribcage, I'm figuring out spine vertebrae as small boxes along x, with ribs as curved catmull-rom sweeps arching from the spine down to the floor, varying height and spacing per rib for a half-buried look.

Now I'm laying out the base platform and back wall: base spans roughly 2.4x1.9m, with a wall around 0.95-1.25m tall built from stone tileBox segments to simulate brick texture, including a taller pillar section with a cap, and I'm sizing texel density so the tile pattern repeats properly across each wall segment rather than stretching into one giant tile.

Then I switch to flooring, breaking the 2.4x1.9 slab into several smaller flagstone tileBox pieces (around 0.8x0.08x0.95 each) with randomized texture offsets so the flagstone tile texel scale stays consistent instead of blowing up on one oversized face.

I add a dark underlay slab beneath the flagstones so the mortar gaps between them show through, then lay out the flagstones with slight gaps and offset centers to break up the grid pattern. Now I'm sketching the layout for other floor props -- positioning a spike trap plate near the front and a chest off to one side.

For the chest I settle on x=-0.5 to keep enough clearance from the back wall. Then I'm placing wall torches with iron brackets and angled wooden sticks, one near the left pillar and one above the barrels on the right, sized to sit at a reasonable head height on the wall.

Writing flame particle code...

Now I'm working out barrel placement near the wall, checking radii and positions so the two barrels don't overlap each other or the base edge, adjusting coordinates until the spacing works out.

For the top face of upright barrels I want to add a plank pattern using the x-coordinate to create stripes, though this only applies when the barrel is standing upright, not lying down.

I'm generalizing the end-cap detection to work along any axis by dotting the normal with the barrel's orientation vector, and since the lathe geometry doesn't support scaling directly, I'll write a helper function that scales the outline coordinates manually so I can parameterize barrels by center, scale, axis, and rotation.

I'm weighing whether to add a decal, like a painted skull marking, on one of the barrels but realizing the geometry math for placing a flat plane against the curved lathe surface is tricky given uncertain vertex angles, so I'm deciding to keep it simple rather than risk misaligned placement.

Shifting focus to layout: planning decoration near the chest at a specific position, then sketching out a spike trap's footprint, working through size and coordinate math to keep its base within bounds.

Then I move to scattered bones near the lying barrel—placing a bone pile, a skull, and a rib cage, calculating spine and rib positions along the x and z axes to make the skeletal remains look naturally strewn.

Still placing femur bone coordinates...

Now I'm scattering small decorative details: loose rib bones near the floor, and thinking about adding a second cracked skull atop barrel 2, plus a melted candle stub with a flame card nearby to add visual interest.

Designing the spike trap plate...

Adding spike bases and color details...

I'm placing a pressure plate near the trap with rivet borders and partially extended spikes, then laying out a 4x4 spike grid with randomized heights—some fully extended, some retracted stubs with bone tips, including a few broken ones.

Now I'm building the chest itself: a wooden plank-textured body box with iron bands, topped by a half-buried cylindrical lid rotated along its axis so the rounded top sits above the box.

I'll define a plank-indexing function based on angle around an axis for the lid texture, then handle the end caps separately as iron plates — small thin cylinders placed at the x extremes to cap the barrel visually.

For the metal bands wrapping the body, I'm checking whether their radius slightly exceeds the body's half-depth so they visibly wrap around and protrude a bit, while making sure they don't poke through the bottom.

I'm realizing a full cylinder band would bulge oddly on the body face, so instead I'm switching to extruding a semicircular arch outline along the thin axis to get a cleaner hoop shape.

Still planning paint and iron band placement...

Dark feet boxes sit at corners near base. For the lid, I'm setting up a hinge joint at the back edge with a forward-facing axis, parented to root, so the lid, hasp, and lock plate all move together as a "chestLid" bone while the rest stays on root.

I'm defining a small helper function to place parts on the root bone, keeping the palette under 64 flat colors. For textures, I'm planning pixel-based procedural patterns: brick tiles with alternating offsets and mortar lines plus moss patches, irregular flagstone tiles with cracks and speckling, and a wood grain tile for the chest body, sizing each so the texel scale lines up with the real-world dimensions of the faces they'll cover.

I'm now working out plank striping for the wood texture—seam rows, lighter rows, grain noise streaks, and nail dots—alongside a small pixel-art skull texture for bone, a flame texture, and an iron trap plate texture with holes and rivets aligned to spike positions.

Trying a 28px tile at 0.025 scale to get an exact 0.7 texel size, then adjusting hole positions to land near pixel centers like 5.5, 11.5, 17.5, 22.5.

For the skull, I'm planning a skinBox approach with a bone-speckle pixel texture laid out via a skin UV map, using cranium and jaw boxes sized at roughly 0.128×0.112×0.128m and 0.096×0.048×0.096m respectively, with eye sockets stamped onto the front face, and working out the texture sheet layout dimensions needed to fit both pieces.

Finalizing the eye socket and nose pixel rows, then stamping them in dark color onto the face. Now working out the jaw's teeth pattern as a small pixel grid...

Now I'm sizing and positioning the skull and jaw boxes relative to each other—cranium dimensions from the face layout, jaw sitting just below it, with the jaw resting under the cranium so the skull appears to sit on it, and both pieces rotating together around the yaw axis with the jaw offset slightly forward in local space.

I'm defining a skull helper function that places the cranium and jaw with matching yaw rotation and a scale option for a second smaller skull, then moving on to a femur builder using a rod for the shaft and small spheres as knobs at each end, computing a perpendicular offset from the bone's direction vector to position the knobs correctly.

Next I'm sketching the ribcage: a spine of alternating small cubes for vertebrae, and ribs built as swept tube paths using catmull curves anchored at each spine joint, with tapered radii and rounded or pointed end caps.

Then I move on to designing the wall torch: an iron bracket plate mounted on the wall, a wooden stick as the torch handle, a cloth wrap near the top for the flame head, ring bands around the stick, and an iron cup shape (frustum) to hold the flame.

Now I'm figuring out the flame itself using card geometry and glowing boxes at the torch tip, plus a soot stain decal on the wall above it using a small dithered pixel texture plane offset slightly off the wall surface to avoid z-fighting. I'm also considering whether to add additional sconces or floor torches for more lighting variety.

For the wall structure, I'm laying out the pillar and three wall segments across the span, figuring exact widths and centers so the texture tiles seamlessly, then adding coping caps on top and a stepped, partially broken segment with scattered rubble stones at the base for a ruined look. I'm computing the total height of the assembly including the base, wall, and cap to make sure everything aligns properly.

I'm also planning small decorative touches: subtle moss speckles low on the stone tiles for weathering, and a pixel-art cobweb texture placed diagonally in the corner where the pillar meets the wall to sell the abandoned atmosphere.

Placing the web corner near the pillar, sized to fit inside the wall-pillar corner. I'm giving the plane a light grey color, and planning the chest's spilled coins as small flat gold cylinders.

I'm also adding a red gem octahedron and an iron key near the chest front, and considering popping the lid open slightly by posing the hinge bone with a negative rotation around its forward axis so the front edge lifts up.

Since the body is a solid box, I need to reveal gold once the lid opens, so I'll place a mound of coins and low cones on the top surface of the chest so it's visible when the lid is raised.

I need to make sure lid parts are built and attached before applying the rotation pose, since everything already on the bone will rotate rigidly with it. The hinge joint's default direction matters too, so I'll build lock plate and other fixed elements carefully relative to that.

Let me verify the joint hierarchy and part counts stay reasonable — root and chest lid joints, with the lid hinge positioned above the floor. Tallying up parts across floor, walls, torches, barrels, chest, traps, bones, coins, and rubble keeps me comfortably under the 1000-part budget, so now I'm defining the wood color ramp palette.

Writing color ramps...

Sketching the fire texture pixel grid row by row, carefully keeping each row exactly 10 characters wide with red, orange, yellow, and pale tones placed to form a flame shape.

Writing wood tile texture logic...

Still designing crack and texture logic...

Sketching a small pixel-art skull pattern for the barrel decal...

I'll make barrel 2's X mark an 8x8 cream pixel pattern, then apply it as a decal onto the barrel part using a small offset and lift to avoid z-fighting, checking that the decal function accepts a Part target directly.

Now I'm defining a helper function for painting barrel caps that uses the dot product between a surface normal and an axis vector to detect end caps versus side surfaces.

Still writing stave logic...

Now I'm defining a barrel helper function with a profile outline of points forming the rounded silhouette with sloped rim creases, scaled by size and positioned with lying/yaw orientation.

Working out the hoop rectangle points so the slope error stays negligible, and skipping rivets and decals to keep things simple. I'm setting up barrel size variations — scale 1 and 0.8 for standing barrels, 0.85 with a 0.3 yaw for the lying one — using default lathe segmentation with no smoothing.

Now I'm adjusting lathe crease thresholds and fixing the part parameters to pass axis, color, and bone correctly. I'm also considering making barrel 1 an open-topped hollow shape with a visible water level by adjusting its outline profile.

Still writing lathe outline coordinates...

Now moving to the spike trap, I'm building the plate geometry with a textured iron crop, sizing it to exactly fit the tile pixels on top and sides.

Then I'm adding a stone rim border framing the plate's edges and designing the spike pieces themselves—collar bases plus angled cone shafts rotated 45° to form square diagonals, using layered steel-tone colors for shading.

Still writing spike details...

I'll skip the skull-on-spike idea and other elaborate additions like ribcages or pressure plates—keeping it simpler, just adding scattered pebbles, straw, and small details on the floor.

Adding floor treasure now: scattered gold coins near the chest, a red gem, and a lying key with a torus ring, rod, and tooth shapes, all positioned with slight rotations for natural scatter.

For the treasure pile inside the open chest, I'm placing a flattened red cloth lining, then building heaps of flattened gold spheres with coins and colored gem octahedrons scattered on top, keeping everything within the chest's interior width. I'm also noting that the open lid's underside (the flat bottom face of its arched shape) will be visible as plain wood since the lid rotates upward at roughly -28 degrees.

Now I'm working out the lid's hinge placement at the back of the chest, defining the extrusion outline and orientation so the lid attaches correctly at its pivot point, then moving on to the horizontal reinforcing bands wrapped around the chest body.

Still placing bands and rivets...

For the plinth, I'm skipping the separate feet idea and instead adding a simple darker wooden base box beneath the chest, roughly 0.66 by 0.05 by 0.44, positioned just under the body.

Now I'm working out the chest proportions: body centered with top at CH_TOP = B+0.35, lid sitting right at that seam, and the lock plate/hasp needing to straddle the lid-body boundary so it visually spans both pieces, with the hasp strip attached to the lid front near the arch edge.

I'm adding the gold lock box with keyhole on the body, matching it to the hasp when closed, plus a pair of iron hinge cylinders at the back connecting lid to body.

Now I'm checking for spatial conflicts between the chest, pillar, and rubble blocks — the pillar at x[-1.2,-.9] overlaps the chest's footprint, so I'm shifting the chest to x=-0.55 to clear it, then placing a torch nearby above the chest.

For the stage area, I'm positioning rubble and stone chips near the barrels and wall segments, checking that nothing collides with the spike trap or the broken third wall segment.

Checking torch heights against the wall's broken top — torch 2 at x=.85 needs its flame tip to sit roughly level with or just above the wall segment's top edge; adjusting base/tip y-values so the torches read as standing in front of the wall rather than clipping through it. Now setting per-segment wall heights for the broken top profile.

Adding stone coping on the two intact wall segments while leaving segment 3 broken with rubble, plus a pillar with a cap and base block positioned just outside the wall, sized so its texture tiling stays proportional. Deciding to skip extra details like grooves, chains, or shackles for now, and confirming the tileBox function's parameters for size, tiling, and randomization.

Now I'm sketching a small helper function for creating textured parts attached to the skeleton, then planning a candle on top of barrel2 — working out the barrel's top height so I can place a wax candle with a drip base and a glowing flame card at the correct position.

Writing skull placement logic...

Checking box face orientation to confirm the front faces align correctly at yaw zero, then moving to the torch placement function, setting wall-mounted coordinates and building a small rod/stick shape with a wood color ramp.

Still writing torch geometry...

I accept vector or array inputs for positions. For the soot mark, I'm placing a plane on the wall just behind the torch flame, positioning it so it only overlaps the region directly above the torch rather than the whole wall surface.

Checking that the plane sits above the torch mounting plate without overlapping, and confirming the soot texture's fan shape opens upward and narrows toward the bottom as intended, colored with a dark soot tone. I'm planning the cobweb plane the same way, and now considering whether to add a warm glow decal on the floor beneath the torch using a flat dithered orange texture plane.

I decide a sparse dithered orange speckle might just look like noise, so I'll skip the floor glow pool. Instead I'll add small glowing yellow spark cubes near each torch flame, a few per torch at slightly randomized positions, and leave floor extras like pebbles or bone dust aside for now.

Now I'm placing a flat thin puddle of water near barrel1, positioning it slightly above the flagstone surface to avoid z-fighting, and considering a similar dark red flattened pool near the trap for a blood effect.

I'm skipping extra decor like coiled chains and straw, and instead placing a loose pile of bones in the open area near the pillar, working out the spine and rib positions for a ribcage layout.

Still placing bones...

Adjusting femur C's start position slightly, then scattering small loose bone fragments (jaw bits, tiny rods) around the skull region using randomized placement within a safe bounding box. Now I'm thinking through TypeScript import requirements, making sure to only import what's actually used to avoid strict unused-variable errors.

Setting up the module imports from the kit and core builder utilities, then starting to define the build function with wood constants, a root joint, a seeded RNG, and a helper for placing parts with consistent typing.

Writing wood texture pixel art...

Still writing tile textures...

Now I'm setting up the skull sprite sheet, computing layout for cranium and jaw faces, then filling each face region with a bone-colored gradient and dithering, checking that the TypeScript types for the face/rect iteration hold up correctly.

Working out the bone color palette and crack detail, then moving to the fire pixel art and barrel stamps before assembling the full scene code, including a helper function for drawing cylindrical bone rods between joint points.

Writing knob and rib geometry...

Still shaping the broken ribs near the floor, then sweeping a tapered tube through those points with a catmull-rom curve and linear radius falloff for the final mesh.

Now I'm adding alternating vertebra boxes along a spine bone, then building a gold pile from randomized spheres flattened into coin-stack shapes, scattered around a center point with scaled height, topped off with tilted cylindrical coins.

Next I'm setting up three gems, posing the lid at a -35 angle, and adding barrel mark decals plus a meta description. I'm checking type compatibility for a fill color parameter that can be a string or Paint object, confirming cellPaint resolves correctly.

Now I'm constructing stone wall segments using a tiled brick texture function, placing each wall segment at computed positions with row-based mortar offsets to keep bricks aligned, alternating the pattern by row for a realistic masonry look.

I'm working out the staggered brick offset math to center bricks evenly on each wall face, then sizing a pillar's tiled sides and top cap to fit within texture bounds, and adding a coping piece along the top edge. For the floor, I'm placing an underlay box and then tiling individual stone flagstones across the floor area, checking that each flagstone's face dimensions and vertical position align properly with the texture tiling grid.

Now I'm confirming the flagstone edges fit within the floor boundaries and considering a slightly darker stone trim color for the floor's side faces, then moving on to building candle flames with glowing card geometry, torch tips using a frame-based glow helper, and small spark cube particles.

Adding torch glow cores and barrel decals...

I'm working out where to position water inside the open barrel, calculating its local height relative to the barrel's base and rim so it sits just below the lip.

Still writing barrel geometry...

Yes, lathe axis handles yaw fine with ends normal along the axis. I'm sketching the chest lid paint using angular banding to fake plank seams, then similarly sketching flat speckled paint for the base plinth and composing the full box with iron paint accents and spike positions along the top edges.

Still writing spike geometry... I'm placing iron collar plates, cone-shaped spike bases with blood-tipped variants at specific indices, corner rivets, and finally a key ring made from a small torus near the chest front, double-checking variable naming so loop counters don't collide with the RNG helper.

Now I'm positioning the scattered coins relative to the chest and femur bones so they land in the right trap zone, then laying out the key's shaft as a thin rod between the ring and a set of key-bit boxes using gold-tinted iron coloring. I'm confirming the rod and sweep helper signatures accept radius and style options correctly before finalizing torch rod paths with a lerp helper for intermediate points, then wrapping up constant definitions for the iron paint color used throughout the build.
